newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Agreement ends S.Africa truckers' strike--union.
newsitem.headline: Agreement ends S.Africa truckers' strike--union.

text.p: The three-day-old national truckers' strike ended on Friday after employers and the seven unions organised in the sector agreed on wages during drawn-out mediation.
Harald Harvey, the Transport and General Workers' Union assistant general secretary, said an agreement was signed at about 1930 GMT on Friday.
"We've just signed it now. It's a great victory -- that's the only way to describe it," Harvey told Reuters.

The strike over wages and working conditions in the 36,000-strong sector started on Wednesday and was the first in the industry in 50 years. It was also the first under the new Labour Relations Act which came into effect earlier this month.
According to union officials the strike took the form of pickets at trucking companies which resorted to employing scab labour.
Employers said the strike disrupted most sectors of the economy as some companies ground to a complete standstill while others managed to keep on running.

The final agreement was mediated by the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration (CCMA), a dispute resolution body which provides statutory dispute resolution services under the new Labour Relations Act.

The CCMA stepped in to mediate between the parties on the eve of the strike on Tuesday in a bid to resolve the wage deadlock. After initial deadlocks, talks continued on Thursday and resumed again on Friday afternoon.
Harvey said the agreement was for a 13 percent across the board increase on actual wages effective from January 1.

On minimum wages agreement was reached for a 12 percent hike for Gauteng province centred on Johannesburg, other urban areas including Durban and Cape Town 16 percent and for small towns, 17.5 percent.
The union's original wage demand was between 14 to 18 percent across-the-board although it presented an unmandated 12.5 percent wage offer to employers at the beginning of the week.
Also at the beginning of the week employers revised their original offer from nine to 10 percent.
Harald said some truckers had returned to work after the signing of the agreement with employers on Friday night. The bulk of truckers would however be back on work on Monday.
